item.title: 'Generational theft': Experts say senator's plan could add $45 trillion to debt
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A new plan to pay Social Security benefits with even more government borrowing has drawn harsh pushback from budget experts, who note it would make America's debt exponentially worse and fail to fix the underlying problem. Republican Sen. Ron Johnson introduced a bill this week that would forestall any cuts in benefits by authorizing transfers from the US Treasury in the event of a shortfall in Social Security's main Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OADSI) Trust Fund. The bill has little chance of passage, but this week's contretemps illustrates Washington's current lack of readiness to confront the Social Security shortfall that is projected to be felt during the next presidential term. Read more: Retirement planning by age: The complete guide for your 20s-70s An array of budget experts dismissed Johnson's plan as unserious. They say solutions are urgently needed before the program is depleted in about six years — but that this isn't it. "Let's be clear: Senator Johnson's proposal would add $45 trillion (!) to the national debt through three decades," wrote Jessica Riedl, a budget and tax fellow at the Brookings Institution, calling it "generational theft." Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., talks with reporters outside the Senate chamber during a vote at the US Capitol on Aug. 7, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Rod Lamkey, Jr.) AP Photo/Rod Lamkey "This isn't Social Security reform. It isn't even a nothingburger. It is actually anti-reform," said Douglas Holtz-Eakin, a former director of the Congressional Budget Office, calling it "a terrible step in the wrong direction." Johnson, for his part, was unapologetic, writing on X , "My Stop Scaring Seniors Act simply prevents Social Security benefits from being reduced when the trust fund is depleted." Read more: How much do you really need to save for retirement? But with the US already more than $40 trillion in debt , Johnson's bill would need to be funded by more government borrowing which — the bill specifies — would not count toward US debt ceiling calculations. "Not only does the legislation automate congressional malfeasance, it evades any congressionally set limits on that malfeasance," Holtz-Eakin added. The Social Security program's trustees currently estimate that the program will face a shortfall by 2032, which, under current law, would force benefits to be cut by roughly 22% . Experts for years have urged lawmakers to avert this shortfall through some combination of increasing revenue and the hot-button topic of reducing benefits. Social Security is funded through payroll taxes. One fix often pushed by Democrats is to raise the taxable income cap, which rises to $192,300 in 2027 . Earnings above that amount are not subject to the tax, a break for wealthier Americans. A Social Security Administration sign is seen in front of the agency's headquarters in Maryland in 2025. (Wesley Lapointe/For The Washington Post via Getty Images) The Washington Post via Getty Images But Johnson's plan sidesteps any tax increases or benefit cuts by authorizing more borrowing, which the budget hawks at the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget estimate would have a long-term price tag of $190 trillion over the next 75 years in inflation-adjusted terms. Just passing the bill, the group says, could spark a debt crisis. " We usually say that inaction is the worst option when it comes to Social Security, but now we found something even worse," Maya MacGuineas, the group's president, said in a scathing review, calling it "a cynical pander that ducks all the real decisions we need to confront." The shock from budget experts has done little to dampen Johnson's push and his critiques of the overall program. Johnson, who chairs the Senate Budget Committee until Democrats take over in 2027, also released a memo this week that called Social Security "a Legal Ponzi Scheme." "You can't fix it," he said in an appearance on Fox News . "You just shut it down and hope that you can recover some of your money." An earlier version of this story listed an previous employer for Riedl. She is now a fellow at the Brookings Institution. Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. This article originally appeared on Yahoo Finance at https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article/generational-theft-harsh-pushback-follows-a-plan-to-fund-social-security-with-more-government-borrowing-160247441.html

item.title: FBI investigates apparent breach of nationwide crime database used by police
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A seal reading "Department of Justice Federal Bureau of Investigation" is displayed on the J. Edgar Hoover FBI building in Washington, DC, on August 9, 2022. - Stefani Reynolds/AFP/Getty Images/File The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its nationwide criminal information database that serves as a lifeline between federal, state and local law enforcement, two people briefed on the investigation said. The intrusion of the National Crime Information Center by apparent hackers is the second such breach in recent months. The NCIC database is used by law enforcement nationwide to share information on warrants and background checks. The discovery of the latest intrusion in recent days comes as the Trump administration has sought to assuage public concern about the nation’s cybersecurity amid a series of high profile outages affecting banks, the National Security Agency and the FAA’s air traffic control system. The FBI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. On Thursday, after bureau officials learned of the latest cybersecurity incident, FBI Director Kash Patel appeared on Fox News to tout the FBI’s cybersecurity work. Patel used the appearance to discuss an operation completed months ago aimed at urging companies to update their systems and prevent hackers from getting to their sensitive data. Patel referred to Operation Winter Shield as if it was still in the works, and touted the current administration for making updates to key systems to protect the nation’s critical infrastructure. “Other administrations could have made these updates, but they didn’t,” he said. “We are staying ahead of the curve and making up for lost time.” The NCIC database is one of the most critical information-sharing systems in law enforcement, a former FBI official who led investigations into cybercriminal groups told CNN. “Every day, officers across the country rely on NCIC to identify wanted fugitives, check for outstanding warrants, and access information that can directly impact officer and public safety. My concern isn’t simply whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.” Prior hacks A September attack by a group called ShinyHunters targeted sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website. A Canadian cybersecurity researcher and author has been arrested and faces charges related to the ShinyHunters breach. After the ShinyHunters breach, some FBI employees felt left in the dark about whether they were affected by the data theft and underwhelmed by the security resources being offered to victims, CNN previously reported . In an earlier breach in 2023, hackers breached a computer system the FBI’s New York field office used in child sexual exploitation investigations, including a system used to store images related to the Jeffrey Epstein probe, CNN previously reported. CNN’s Sean Lyngaas contributed to this report. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/20/politics/fbi-hacked-again-target-crime-database

item.title: The next Senate has 98 names. 2 incoming governors can fill in the final blanks.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The last undecided Senate race finally got a winner on Tuesday night when Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan to give her party its ninth flipped seat this midterm cycle. Peltola’s win, which came more than two weeks after Election Day, means the final balance of power in the Senate is set. When the new Congress convenes for the first time in January, Democrats will control 56 seats, and Republicans will hold 44 seats. But there are still two important questions that remain unanswered about the next Senate caucus. As it stands, we only know the identities of 98 of the 100 senators who will serve in the upcoming Congress, and it could be weeks before we find out who those last two pivotal lawmakers will be. That’s because two current senators, Tennessee Republican Marsha Blackburn and Minnesota Democrat Amy Klobuchar, were each elected governor of their home states. They will need to leave the Senate to assume their new positions. Laws in Tennessee and Minnesota give governors the power to temporarily fill Senate vacancies. That means Blackburn and Klobuchar can each choose their own successor as one of their first acts as governor if they wait to resign from the Senate until shortly before they’re sworn in. Both have indicated they plan to do so but have offered very few clues about who they might consider. It’s highly unlikely that either of them would select a replacement from the opposition party, so the partisan split in the Senate probably won’t change. But their decisions will still carry a lot of weight. Whoever they choose will occupy two of the most important legislative seats in the U.S. government and could play a significant role in defining the ideological direction of their respective parties. Volunteers in Tennessee Blackburn, who has represented Tennessee in the Senate since 2019, announced her bid for governor in August 2025, just nine months after winning reelection to a second Senate term. This year’s gubernatorial race was much closer than Republicans in the Volunteer State are accustomed to, but Blackburn was still able to defeat her Democratic challenger, Jerri Green, by more than 50,000 votes. She is the first woman elected to the state’s top office. Blackburn is a staunch conservative and Trump ally. She opened her first gubernatorial campaign video by saying, “Trump is back. America is blessed and Tennessee: better than ever.” Her MAGA credentials suggest she’s likely to select a successor with a similar profile, but that won’t be certain until her choice is formally announced. Throughout the campaign, Blackburn repeatedly declined to answer questions about who she might choose to replace her but said early on in the process that she intended to make the decision herself, rather than leaving it up to outgoing Republican Gov. Bill Lee. That hadn’t changed in the weeks since she was formally elected. She told Fox News on Nov. 15 that she hadn’t made up her mind and didn’t yet have a “short list” of potential replacements. “I’m focused on finishing the work in the Senate and transitioning to governor,” she said. Blackburn’s coyness hasn’t stopped speculation about who her selection might be. In the days after Democrats’ decisive midterm performance earlier this month — which many top Republicans attributed to voters' dissatisfaction with the war in Iran — rumors began to spread that Blackburn might choose embattled Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to fill her seat. Those rumors were quickly refuted by sources close to Blackburn. The two names that have been most frequently suggested as Blackburn’s replacement are former Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs and U.S. Rep. Tim Burchett. Jacobs turned to politics after a long career in professional wrestling, where he performed as the horror-themed character Kane. He told Fox News in September that it would be a “huge honor” to be Blackburn’s chosen successor and he would “consider it very seriously” if asked. Burchett, who represents Tennessee’s deep red Second District in the House of Representatives, has said he “absolutely” wants to be considered for the position. He has also made clear that he intends to run for the Senate in 2028 against Blackburn’s pick if she chooses someone other than him. Blackburn is scheduled to be sworn in as governor on Jan. 16 and would likely appoint her replacement shortly after taking office. Whoever she chooses will hold her seat until the 2028 general election, when a special election will be held to decide who will finish out the remaining two years of her term. A battle brewing in Minnesota When Minnesota’s Democratic Gov. Tim Walz abruptly dropped his bid for a third term in January, reports immediately began to circulate that Klobuchar was considering launching a bid to replace him. She made it official a few weeks later. A former presidential candidate with a strong record of success in statewide races, Klobuchar quickly became the frontrunner in the Minnesota governor's race. She easily defeated Republican Lisa Demuth on Election Day. She will be the first woman to serve as governor of her state as well when she’s sworn in on Jan. 4. Like Blackburn, Klobuchar has said she intends to choose her own successor and has remained mum on who she may be considering. One name that can be crossed off the list is Walz, who said he would “rather eat glass” than take over her Senate seat. Under Minnesota law, Klobuchar’s successor would fill her seat on a temporary basis until November 2027, when a special election will be held to decide who will finish the remaining three years of her term. Because of that short time frame, Klobuchar has described the appointment as an “interim position.” “It would be for about a year," she told a local news station last month. Nothing in Minnesota law bars appointees from running to keep their seat, but there is some recent history of governors filling vacancies with lawmakers who promise not to campaign for reelection. Replacements often end up holding on to their seats, however. Minnesota’s other senator, Tina Smith, was appointed to her seat in 2018 and has been reelected twice since then. Smith is retiring when her term ends in January. Klobuchar could insist that her successor pledge to serve only as a temporary placeholder, but she hasn’t said whether she might disqualify potential candidates who decline to do so. Her selection, and the Senate race that will follow in November, could say a lot about the ideological direction of the Democratic Party. Midwest swing states were home to some of the most tightly contested midterm primary battles between progressive and moderate candidates anywhere in the country. Minnesota’s Senate primary was won by the more left-leaning candidate, Peggy Flanagan. The same thing happened in nearby Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed eked out a primary win over moderate Haley Stevens. Both Flanagan and El-Sayed won their general election races earlier this month. item.title: Democrats put Trump admin on notice over alleged document destruction
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Ranking member Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at Rayburn building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing on Wednesday, February 11. - Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc./Getty Images/File Democrats and the White House are already in a showdown over alleged document destruction — and the party hasn’t even taken control of Congress yet. Democratic lawmakers and investigators are increasingly concerned that the Trump administration is destroying documents and not adhering to preservation record laws before they take control of Congress, setting off a flurry of letters across the federal government demanding officials properly save documents and turn off auto-delete settings on encrypted messaging applications. The White House has said that Democrats are making claims over document destruction by the administration without evidence, but has also indicated it sees no obligation to comply with their demands to preserve or turn over documents before they gain control of committee gavels in January. The high-stakes standoff is laying the groundwork for a legal fight, as Democrats prepare for far-reaching investigations into the Trump administration and fear that document destruction could hinder their ability to conduct oversight. “What I think you’re seeing in Congress with these document preservation letters is Congress is drawing a line in the sand and maintaining a record so that if people do destroy records they could potentially be prosecuted in a future administration for obstruction of Congress,” Jim Secreto, who worked in the Obama White House Counsel’s office on congressional investigations and compliance with the Presidential Records Act, told CNN. Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, who is in line to chair the House Judiciary Committee, is particularly concerned about the use of Signal by federal employees as a way to circumvent future Democratic oversight. In a series of preservation letters sent to the Department of Justice, Federal Bureau of Investigation, Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Bureau of Prisons, Raskin raised concerns about the potential for document destruction. A White House official told CNN, “We comply with all federal record retention laws and regulations.” A Justice Department official told CNN that the department “follows all legal requirements for the management of federal records involving its official functions and decisions.” They added that the DOJ employees “who work tirelessly to arrest and prosecute criminals will not be intimidated.” A DHS spokesperson similarly said the department “complies with all applicable federal laws, including as it relates to document retention. DHS responds to official correspondence through official channels.” Raskin said in the letters that “there is significant evidence that Trump Administration officials have engaged in the widespread destruction, mutilation, and concealment of government records, seemingly with the express purpose of circumventing federal record preservation laws.” “This attempt to evade transparency extends to the highest levels of federal agencies, including top-ranking law enforcement officials,” he continued. In the letters, Raskin said that a Signal conversation between the general counsel of the FBI and an associate of Donald Trump Jr. appeared to have been set for messages to auto-delete after a week. The Democratic lawmaker said that the conversation concerned “a potential or ongoing investigation involving an individual wanted by federal authorities on health care fraud and related charges.” “This incident, just one of many that have already been reported to our Committee, raises significant concerns that DOJ and FBI officials are openly flouting federal law when it comes to the preservation of official government records,” Raskin said. The panel declined to provide other examples of alleged document destruction with CNN. Judiciary Committee staffers plan to rely on whistleblowers and third parties to help them get the information they seek, but are hoping that the preservation letters sent Friday will put a stop to the use of Signal and auto-delete settings for official work by federal employees. “We want them to be on notice that this behavior is wrong. And if they are doing it, and especially if they continue doing it, we will draw inferences from your destruction of evidence. That’s something that every litigate is familiar with, both in the civil and criminal context,” a Democratic source familiar told CNN. Other Democrats are also raising concerns of alleged document destruction and federal employees using encrypted messaging applications without properly storing them. Congressional sources preparing investigations into Trump’s construction projects around Washington told CNN whistleblowers have warned that key paperwork has already been destroyed before Democrats take power. Democratic Rep. Gregory Meeks warned in his preservation letters earlier this week of document destruction and specifically noted that Signal messages must be properly stored and not subject to automatic deletion. By law, federal employees are required to preserve all records. Federal employees can use encrypted messaging applications like Signal but must correctly store the conversations in compliance with the law. White House Counsel Will Scharf sent letters earlier this week to Democratic committee leaders saying the Trump administration’s position is that no official has to comply with their demands to preserve or turn over documents and information because Democrats do not yet chair the committees, according to a copy of the letter obtained by CNN. On Thursday, Raskin received a preservation letter of his own from US Attorney Aaron Reitz, who accused the Maryland Democrat of weaponizing his investigative efforts without a legislative purpose to go after Trump associates and the administration. Scharf wrote that the purpose of the letters sent by Democrats “is not legitimate oversight but to harass and aggrandize.” “In the days since the November 3, 2026 election, several Ranking Members have sent letters to the Executive Branch demanding documents or information. Some of these letters imply, without evidence, that thousands of United States government employees are conspiring to destroy documents in violation of the Federal Records Act,” he said. In addition to calling on agencies to preserve their documents, Raskin is demanding Attorney General Todd Blanche and other Trump officials open an inquiry into what documents may have been deleted and attempt to recover those records. Even though Democrats don’t yet have the authority to compel document production with subpoena power, these preservation letters serve as a preview of what’s to come, particularly if Democrats regain control of the White House in 2028. “It’s the type of thing that a future Department of Justice could use as evidence in court of intent to destroy records,” Secreto told CNN. Attorney General's Office for nearly two hours during a pretrial hearing in Lexington on Nov. 13, Judge Debra McCaslin ruled Friday, Nov. 20, that Murdaugh's motion to dismiss murder and weapons charges be denied. While Murdaugh's defense attorneys argued in that motion that the lead state investigator in the case, David Owen, presented false or misleading evidence to a local grand jury in order to secure the 2022 indictments, Judge McCaslin ruled that "the remaining unchallenged evidence overwhelmingly established probable cause." Murdaugh was convicted in March 2023 for the June 2021 shooting deaths of his wife Maggie and adult son Paul, but the convictions and resulting two consecutive life sentences were overturned by the S.C. Supreme Court in May over reports of improper jury contact by now-former Colleton County Clerk of Court Rebecca Hill. Murdaugh, who is currently serving lengthy state and federal prison sentences for fraud, has admitted to stealing millions from clients and law partners, but has staunchly denied playing a role in the family killings. Why did Judge McCaslin uphold the Murdaugh murder charges? The alleged false evidence relates to allegations that, in order to obtain the murder indictments, S.C. Law Enforcement Division agent Owen gave false testimony to the Colleton County Grand Jury related to human blood spatter evidence on a shirt Murdaugh was wearing on the night of the killings, as well as false or misleading information about shotgun ammunition patterns that matched one of the missing murder weapons. However, in the concluding remarks of her 11-page order, Judge McCaslin writes: "The Court concludes that Defendant has not established intentional prosecutorial or investigative misconduct that compromised the integrity of the grand jury proceedings. Defendant has not demonstrated that the challenged testimony substantially influenced the grand jury's decision to indict or created grave doubt that the decision was free from such influence. Even if the challenged testimony concerning the blood spatter on the T-shirt and shotgun ammunition were excluded from consideration by the grand jury, the remaining unchallenged evidence overwhelmingly established probable cause. Further, the Court finds no evidence of misuse of the State Grand Jury." In citing her "probable cause" decision, Judge McCaslin cited several other pieces of evidence that were arguably enough to secure an indictment, including "digital timeline records, FBI telemetry analysis, cell phone data, video evidence placing the Defendant at the scene immediately before the homicides, evidence of GSR on the Defendant's raincoat, and circumstantial evidence regarding motive and opportunity," etc. "Dismissal of an indictment based on alleged misconduct during grand jury proceedings is an extraordinary remedy reserved for exceptional circumstances," the order adds. The judge did not take lightly, however, that Owen presented information that later proved false, citing the SLED agent's failure to see an earlier report addressed directly to him that could have shed light on the blood spatter question before he presented incorrect information to the grand jury. "The Court does not take lightly Special Agent Owen's failure to recognize and account for a laboratory report addressed directly to him prior to presenting testimony in this case. Law enforcement bears a fundamental duty to thoroughly review and accurately represent the complete evidentiary record. Oversights of this nature undermine public confidence in the integrity of the criminal justice system. Nevertheless, the Court finds that this failure does not rise to the level of bad faith misconduct warranting dismissal of indictments." This could arguably be a small victory for Murdaugh defense during the retrial, as it casts doubt on Owen's credibility as lead investigator. What happens next in the Murdaugh murder case? The murder case will now continue to retrial beginning the week of April 5, 2027, in Sumter County before Judge McCaslin. The jury questionnaire and selection process is set to begin at the next Murdaugh pretrial hearing on Jan. 20 in Sumter. Why did Alex Murdaugh seek to dismiss his murder charges? On Aug. 10, Murdaugh's defense team filed a motion to dismiss all four pending criminal indictments against Murdaugh—two murder charges and two related weapons charges — over alleged "false" and "fabricated" evidence and the "...presentation of perjurious testimony and fabricated evidence to the grand jury, creating a colorable claim of prosecutorial misconduct." The S.C. Attorney General's Office has denied allegations that Owens knowingly lied to the jury, arguing that he presented the information he had at the time in the evolving case. 'The grand jury was misled greatly' During the hearing, Murdaugh attorney Jim Griffin, displaying a lengthy PowerPoint presentation, alleged that SLED knew by August 2021 that there was no human blood spatter on the shirt, and cited a Nov. 10, 2021, lab report addressed to Owen stating the same result, but Owen still gave the grand jury the false information in July of 2022. "There's no way to claim that this (false blood spatter evidence) had no influence on the grand jury," Griffin said. "The grand jury was misled greatly when they returned this indictment." However, the State claimed that Owen did not see that report until November of 2022. The State also pointed out that, while the SLED lab report indicated there was no human blood, an independent expert gave an opinion that stains on the shirt were consistent with blood spatter. 'This was all very, very compelling evidence' Murdaugh's defense also argued that Owen told the grand jury that other weapons found on the property were loaded exactly like the murder weapon - first a buckshot shell, then a birdshot "turkey load," which they said was also false. SC Deputy Attorney General Creighton Waters argued that the gun Murdaugh had in his possession when police arrived at the crime scene on the night of June 7, 2021, was loaded with one buckshot and a birdshot, although it was not a turkey shell. Other guns found at the Murdaugh family home had mixed combinations of birdshot shells. Waters also argued that the Grand Jury was presented with many other "compelling" pieces of evidence when they returned the murder indictments, including a cell phone video that puts Murdaugh at the crime scene despite his original claims that he wasn't there. "This was all very, very compelling evidence," Waters said. Judge sets key deadlines for upcoming Murdaugh retrial process Even as the prospect of dismissal remained a possibility, Judge McCaslin continued to move ahead in the retrial process and set several upcoming deadlines: Jan. 20, 2027, will be the deadline for both sides to agree on the juror questionnaire to be mailed in January to potential Sumter County jurors. This is also the date of the next pretrial conference, which will be held in Sumter. March 1, 2027, is the deadline for both parties to present the list of expert witnesses they intend to call at trial. Math's "white whale" may have just been cracked with the help of Anthropic's Claude. J Studios/Getty Images A mathematician said on Friday that he cracked one of the biggest problems in mathematics. Levent Alpöge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, said he used Claude to solve it. Mathematicians told Business Insider the result hasn't been fully verified yet. One of the biggest open problems in all of mathematics may have just been cracked by a mathematician using AI. Levent Alpöge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, said on Friday that he solved the Riemann Hypothesis, which involves prime numbers, using Claude. "I guided us to the right situation analogous to that toy setting, and then Claude began to leave me in awe," Alpöge said in a post on his website. "Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line." Though Alpöge's solution has yet to be formally verified, leading scholars in the field told Business Insider on Friday that should it stand, this would be the biggest breakthrough in math yet. "If it holds up, it's an extremely big deal," said Steven Strogatz , a math professor at Cornell. "This is the Moby Dick of Mathematics, the great white whale." Sergei Gukov , a math professor at Caltech, called the claim a "HUGE deal." "This is not a small potato," he said. "RH was the biggest problem in math." Strogatz said Alpöge's solution has been verified by a computer-based system, but added that it sometimes makes mistakes . "So it's fair to say that the claimed proof has not yet been independently verified," he said. The Riemann Hypothesis was first proposed 167 years ago by a German mathematician named Bernhard Riemann. It proposes a predicted distribution for how often prime numbers appear alongside other numbers. The task of proving the hypothesis is a Millennium Prize Problem , meaning that solving it earns a mathematician a $1 million prize. The Navier-Stokes equations, which OpenAI has said it solved, are also in the Millennium Prize category. Alpöge's solution is, by his own admission, incredibly long and complicated. The solution's written proof comprises more than 250,000 pages, Alpöge said. Terence Tao, a leading scholar based at UCLA, said in a post on his website Friday that "digesting" the proposed solution "will take some time."
